title: Awesome Robot RSI
description: Recent papers on robot recursive self-improvement.

papers.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
papers.summary: Refines robot expert programs through simulator rollouts against a frozen judge, retaining verified experts to generate demonstrations. Independently reviewed video renders turn those rollouts into action-labelled data for training real-robot policies.
papers.loop: Write a task expert → run development-seed rollouts → use the frozen judge’s verdicts to revise controller code → evaluate on hidden held-out seeds → retain verified experts and handoff records → generate and independently review demonstrations for policy training.
papers.setting: Simulator task reconstruction from one real calibration episode; action-labelled video rendering; pi0.5 policies trained on 100 episodes per task and evaluated on five physical PiPER-arm tasks in the original and an unseen appearance condition.
papers.evidence: Section 4.4 describes controller-program development through judged simulator rollouts followed by hidden-seed admission. The released expert harness persists handoff bundles and a content-addressed verified-expert library. Figure 3 and Appendix A route rejections to the responsible stage while retaining prior attempts. Author-reported real-robot outcomes are 93/100 successes for farm-data policies versus 84/100 for teleoperation data, and 87/100 versus 46/100 under an unseen tablecloth and coloured lighting. These results evaluate generated-data training, not repeated autonomous policy-weight improvement or demonstrated long-term capability-layer evolution. The separate capability-evolution module’s example evaluator verifies software behaviour only.

figure.alt: PyRUA-DataFarm Figure 3: grounding, task and expert code, simulated episodes, video rendering and admission, with rejected outputs routed back to the responsible stage.
figure.credit: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma et al., PyRUA-DataFarm, Figure 3. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: TAMPAgent: Agentic Belief-Space Planning for Mobile Manipulation
papers.summary: Combines an agent with belief-space task-and-motion planning. A single-task self-improvement study retains memory between attempts, allowing earlier failures to guide later solutions.
papers.loop: Execute a mobile-manipulation attempt → save observations and lessons in memory → reset and retry with that memory → compare completion and token use.
papers.setting: Simulated RBY1 and G1 mobile manipulation, plus physical RBY1 and G1 demonstrations; the repeated-attempt study uses simulation task T9.
papers.evidence: Figure 10 and Section 4 test recursive self-improvement on one task. TAMPAgent and GaP succeed on attempt three, CaP on attempt four; TAMPAgent uses 42%/31% fewer uncached input tokens. This narrow experiment does not establish cross-task continual improvement.

figure.alt: TAMPAgent Figure 4: agent hypotheses, planner constraints, tool certification, execution and replanning.
figure.credit: Utkarsh A. Mishra et al., TAMPAgent, Figure 4. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.summary: A coding model studies robot rollouts and repeatedly improves the tools, control routines and persistent memory around a frozen VLA policy. The resulting harness is evaluated on unseen scenes and tasks.
papers.loop: Run the frozen policy inside its harness → inspect rollout traces and failures → edit control routines, tools and persistent memory → evaluate and refine the harness → test on held-out episodes.
papers.setting: Simulation across LIBERO-Pro, VLABench, SimplerEnv and RoboCasa-365, with held-out scene and task splits.
papers.evidence: Figure 2 and Sections 3–4 describe automatic harness optimization without model-weight updates. Author-reported mean held-out success rises from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks. These are simulation evaluations, not official RoboDojo results.

figure.alt: RoboArchitect Figure 2: a coding model diagnoses rollouts and evolves a frozen policy’s harness and persistent memory.
figure.credit: Shengguang Wu et al., RoboArchitect, Figure 2.

papers.title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control
papers.summary: Retains development success statistics to route among reusable robot policies, including ASPIRE’s refined and evolved code. It evaluates this memory and a failure-judging gate on held-out episodes.
papers.loop: Evaluate reusable policies on development seeds → retain per-task success and efficiency statistics as route memory → dispatch and escalate among policies on held-out seeds → compare with source-policy and routing ablations.
papers.setting: LIBERO-Pro, RoboTwin 2.0 and BEHAVIOR-1K simulation, with separate physical-robot demonstrations.
papers.evidence: Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendix A.2 evaluate frozen generated-policy libraries, including ASPIRE Fix and Evo. On ASPIRE’s 59-task LIBERO-Pro subset, route memory lifts author-reported success from 66.3% to 71.9%; the judge gate reaches 74.9%. This is evaluation of persistent routing over improved policies, not evidence that the runtime autonomously rewrites policies at test time.

figure.alt: REA Figure 3: asynchronous policy dispatch from route memory and a boundary-triggered judge gate, compared with blocking control loops.
figure.credit: Pengfei Zhou et al., REA, Figure 3. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

papers.title: BioAgent: Self-Directed Skill Acquisition and Capability Growth for Long-Horizon Laboratory Protocols
papers.summary: Uses execution records to identify missing laboratory skills, request human teaching when needed, and validate new or revised skills. Accepted experience supports offline policy updates and reusable task packages.
papers.loop: Match protocol requirements to validated skills → identify a capability gap from execution evidence → construct or revise a skill, requesting human demonstrations when needed → validate the sequence → retain accepted experience for offline learning and future protocols.
papers.setting: Physical Monte 02 dual-arm laboratory protocols with 20 and 31 ordered skill calls; 25 atomic skills.
papers.evidence: The second protocol reuses 17 skill types unchanged, revises two implementations and adds five skill types. Complete-task success is 66%/58% over 50 runs per protocol with recovery. Requirements are human-reviewed and acquisition can require teaching; this is not fully autonomous skill discovery.

figure.alt: BioAgent Figure 2: requirement analysis, capability matching, targeted teaching, execution verification and offline learning return validated skills to future planning.
figure.credit: Gaojing Zhang et al., BioAgent, Figure 2.

papers.title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents
papers.summary: Coding agents improve a frozen teacher’s tools, memory and recovery, keeping edits that pass paired statistical tests. Teacher trajectories then train small robot agents that reuse the evolved harness.
papers.loop: Read frozen-teacher execution trajectories → propose a harness edit → accept only after a pre-registered paired A/B gate → freeze the final harness → collect reasoning and recovery traces → distill small student policies.
papers.setting: RoboTwin, Guava and LIBERO-Pro training simulations; unseen simulation benchmarks and SO-ARM101 demonstrations.
papers.evidence: Humans predefine rules and budget; frontier coding agents propose harness edits. Table 1 reports teacher success from 33.4% at H1 to 63.6% at the final harness on 500 RoboTwin episodes, and 62.8% for the final 4B student. Students are trained separately for each harness version; teacher weights remain frozen.

figure.alt: TinyAstral Figure 2: statistically gated harness evolution, teacher-trajectory distillation and deployment of small students in the same harness.
figure.credit: Kehong Gong et al., TinyAstral, Figure 2.

papers.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
papers.summary: Builds audited robot simulations and studies agents that retain notes and code across repeated attempts. RoboWorld also evaluates privileged coaching and VLA training from code-generated demonstrations.
papers.loop: Execute robot attempts in a simulation → retain notes and code in context → reset to the same start → revise subsequent attempts. Separately, creation and audit agents iteratively repair simulation and task code and share lessons across simulations.
papers.setting: RoboWorld: 25 simulations, 175 training environments and 25 test environments; robot manipulation, mobile and humanoid embodiments in simulation.
papers.evidence: Section 5 studies persistent in-context learning across three attempts, qualitative coaching from a privileged teacher, and transfer from privileged experience. Learning experiments use 11 simulations; code-generated demonstrations train pi0.5 on two gift-box tasks. Initial frontier agents complete no test tasks. These simulation studies do not establish broad real-world transfer.

figure.alt: Gym-Anything Figure 2: simulation selection, creation and audit, task generation, and learning from repeated attempts and privileged experience.
figure.credit: Pranjal Aggarwal and Sean Welleck, Gym-Anything for Robotics, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: Ask to Evolve: A Unified Harness for Lifelong Embodied Navigation with Hybrid Action Space and Persistent Memory
papers.summary: Combines navigation with active requests for guidance and persistent spatial memory. It retains place descriptions, observations and interaction history to improve later visits and tasks.
papers.loop: Navigate and observe execution feedback → ask for guidance when uncertain → store spatially grounded observations and dialogue → retrieve and revise that memory on later visits → evaluate repeated navigation.
papers.setting: Eight simulated navigation benchmarks spanning four task families, plus multi-day physical navigation.
papers.evidence: Figure 2 describes retained place memory linking poses and supporting evidence across tasks. Author-reported R2R revisit SPL rises from 82.23 to 93.31. Active guidance can come from a multimodal guide in simulation or people in physical experiments; results do not imply fully unassisted learning.

figure.alt: EvoLife Figure 2: hybrid navigation actions, active interaction and persistent spatial memory retain experience for future tasks.
figure.credit: Kai Sheng et al., EvoLife, Figure 2.

papers.title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
papers.summary: Benchmarks household robot agents that revise and retain reusable control tools from execution feedback. Compares recursive self-improvement across task-level capabilities and open-ended home scenarios.
papers.loop: Plan, execute and verify household actions → identify failures → refine reusable control functions → retain successful tools across attempts → reevaluate task and scenario performance.
papers.setting: AgiBot G1 household robot; 50 simulated home layouts, task-level evaluations and four open-ended scenario types; matched simulation and real-world subsets.
papers.evidence: Section 2.3 defines the code-planner/code-policy/code-verifier + RSI architecture with persistent tool improvements. Section 3.3 and Figure 6 compare three coding agents over successive RSI iterations. Simulation and real-world scores are separate; the public evaluator and clients are not a reproduction of every paper experiment.

figure.alt: RobotAgentBench Figure 1: household environments, composable tasks and task-level and open-ended scenario evaluation.
figure.credit: Lingjun Mao et al., RobotAgentBench, Figure 1. CC BY 4.0.

papers.name: WorldScape-R²SI
papers.title: R²SI: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via a Bi-Level Agentic System with Agent–Model Co-Evolution
papers.date_note: Technical report date; the project was announced on 2026-10-17.
papers.summary: Uses a Robot Agent to execute tasks and a Recursion Agent to improve reusable skills and train the reactive model from rollout feedback.
papers.loop: Execute → review rollouts → revise Skills and/or train the reactive model → test against acceptance criteria → release a versioned update → execute again.
papers.evidence: The technical report and official RoboDojo-Sim snapshot report Average Score 46.58 and Success Rate 39.35%. The project page retains its historical October 17 rank-one claim; the October 28 snapshot ranks the system fourth. Reported simulations and selected case studies do not establish broad real-world performance.

figure.caption: Figure 1: a Recursion Agent tests and releases harness and reactive-model updates for an inner Robot Agent.
figure.credit: Manifold AI Team, R²SI technical report, Figure 1.
figure.extraction: Rendered only the original Figure 1 region from PDF page 2, without redrawing or changing its content.
figure.alt: Figure 1: a Recursion Agent tests and releases harness and reactive-model updates for an inner Robot Agent.

papers.source_catalogue: RoboDojo-Sim Agent leaderboard top five; supplemental primary-source verification.
papers.setting: RoboDojo-Sim manipulation; Agent + World Action Model.

papers.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
papers.summary: Improves a planning harness from robot rollouts while keeping the low-level VLA fixed, helping the agent track task history and recover from failures.
papers.loop: Execute with a frozen VLA → summarize task history and failures → edit planning harness → verify and select → freeze for held-out evaluation.
papers.setting: Simulation · RoboMME history-dependent manipulation
papers.evidence: The selected harness is frozen before held-out testing, while episode context continues to update. The paper reports 51.38% RoboMME success with autonomous selection versus 44.38% without self-evolution. The Apache-2.0 implementation uses an external Codex planner and the released RoboMME grounded-subgoal π0.5 checkpoint; model weights and benchmark assets are downloaded separately. Evaluation is in simulation.

figure.alt: SERA method: a task-history harness around a frozen VLA is revised and selected using rollout feedback.
figure.credit: Tingwen Du et al., From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
papers.summary: Evaluates how robot agents improve across repeated attempts, measuring learning speed, interaction cost, and generalization.
papers.loop: Evaluate the initial agent → repeated budgeted attempts with persistent code/tools/memory → revise between attempts → measure gain timing, best scores, cost and generalization.
papers.setting: Simulation · 18 RoboDojo dual-arm tasks; released generalization code covers four tasks
papers.evidence: The paper evaluates 18 RoboDojo manipulation tasks with fixed model weights and interaction budgets; agents revise persistent code, tools and memory for up to 17 improvement rounds. The released generalization-study implementation covers four tasks rather than the paper’s full 18. Best-score metrics include partial progress and differ from native binary success; capability associations are observational.

figure.alt: PhysRSI-Eval workflow: initial evaluation is followed by budgeted attempts with persistent skills, tools, policies, and memory.
figure.credit: Zekai Li et al., Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.name: HexaShell
papers.title: HexaShell: A Universal Harness for Robot Coding Agents in Simulation and the Real World
papers.summary: Shares a 14-tool harness across simulators and real robots. An analysis agent drafts reusable task skills from earlier execution records, with human review before evaluation.
papers.loop: Run robot episodes → analyze recorded code, outputs and images → draft evidence-backed Markdown task skills → human review and format checks → retain skills for later evaluation. The earlier Preview used an optimizer to repair task-specific code tools.
papers.evidence: arXiv v3, Sections 2.4 and E.6, describes 205 retained task skills drafted from earlier run records and reviewed by people. The new shared harness is distinct from HexaShell-TaskTools (the Preview on branch v1.0). Table 6 reports author-run RoboDojo success 85.00% and Score 88.81 with skills, versus 69.92% / 75.73 without skills, under protocols different from the official Preview leaderboard row (46.85% success / 53.18 Score). Physical tests succeed in 76 of 90 episodes. This is human-reviewed skill acquisition, not fully autonomous recursive harness evolution.

figure.alt: HexaShell v3 Figure 2: shared robot API, sandboxed Python execution, grounded perception and adapters, with optional retained task skills.
figure.credit: Hongcheng Gao, Jianshu Zeng et al., HexaShell v3, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

papers.source_catalogue: Awesome-Robot-Use-Agent README, matching HexaShell row; primary sources checked.
papers.setting: RoboDojo, RoboCasa365, LIBERO-PRO and RoboTwin 2.0 simulation; nine tasks on physical dual-arm PiPER-X robots.

related_releases.title: HexaShell: A Universal Harness for Robot Coding Agents in Simulation and the Real World
related_releases.note: Released runtime, sandbox, simulator and real-robot adapters, general tools and human-reviewed task skills; incorporated in arXiv v3 dated November 3. New self-evaluated metrics use protocols different from the official HexaShell-Preview leaderboard entry.

papers.title: InstAgent: A Recursively Self-Improving Agent Operating System for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration
papers.summary: Turns execution-time corrections into validated collaboration behavior trees that can be reused by robot teams. Shared multimodal memory preserves context for later tasks and handoffs.
papers.loop: Execute a collaboration tree → validate handoffs and outcomes → revise and consolidate successful subtrees → retain linked context and procedural experience for future tasks.
papers.setting: Twenty physical heterogeneous multi-robot tasks, evaluated with three high-level models.
papers.evidence: The RSI mechanism updates collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions. The paper evaluates task success, first-attempt completion and efficiency on physical robot teams.

figure.alt: InstAgent Figure 2: BT-based RSI from Skill BTs to collaboration programs. (a) Skill BTs provide reusable capability procedures for task composition. (b) HeteroComposer binds retrieved subtrees to task-specific roles and arguments and composes them with inter-
figure.credit: Haoyang Luo et al., InstAgent, Figure 2.

papers.title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
papers.summary: Revises multi-humanoid coordination code from verified physical transitions while keeping motor skills fixed. Accepted coordination examples and experience guide later runs.
papers.loop: Execute coordination code → verify support, contact, stability and balance → revise rejected behavior from an accepted checkpoint → retain verified coordination experience → evaluate subsequent layouts and experience initialization.
papers.setting: Two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids carrying a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors.
papers.evidence: The paper reports 8 successes among 15 base runs over three backbone families, plus two additional layouts and same-/cross-backbone experience initialization. This is simulation-level coordination evolution with fixed motor skills; motion precision and contact stability remain limitations.

figure.alt: CoEvolve Figure 2: Framework of CoEvolve . The Task Orchestrator commits a team subtask, which the Policy Coder grounds into executable robot policies. Physical verification accepts or rejects the resulting transition; rejected executions trigger structured c
figure.credit: Zicheng Liu et al., CoEvolve, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: CarryOn: A Dual-Loop Harness for Personalized and Reliable Robot Assistance
papers.summary: Keeps revisable user and scene memory for personalized robot assistance. Reflection on failed rollouts refines reusable recovery skills around a frozen VLA policy.
papers.loop: Run a personalized task → monitor physical execution and detect failures → invoke and reflect on recovery → revise reusable recovery skills and persistent context → reuse them in later attempts.
papers.setting: Simulation and physical robot assistance, including preference grounding, action shielding and recovery reuse.
papers.evidence: The paper separates within-rollout supervision from offline refinement of recovery skills. Author-reported recovery success rises from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused. The VLA remains frozen; reported shielding results are separate from recovery-learning results.

figure.alt: CarryOn Figure 2: Two loops, one task context. The planning loop grounds a request in persistent context and dispatches supported subtasks. The execution loop retains the VLA for manipulation, with proactive shielding before hazardous contact and recovery af
figure.credit: Zixuan Wang et al., CarryOn, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: EmbodiedEvo: Self-Evolving Coding Agent For Physical Intelligence
papers.summary: Learns reusable code Skills and diagnostic Lessons in a practice scene, then transfers them to new scenes without weight updates. Learned artifacts for 42 RoboDojo tasks are now public.
papers.loop: Practice in a Playground scene → diagnose physical feedback → revise persistent Skills and Lessons → freeze experience → fresh agents solve unseen Test scenes.
papers.setting: Simulation · RoboDojo-Sim
papers.evidence: Evaluated on RoboDojo-Sim with a Playground/Test protocol. The paper reports an average score of 44.48 and 37.82% success; these results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced here. The official repository added learned Skills and Lessons for 42 RoboDojo tasks on 2026-10-31; these released artifacts do not replace the paper’s fresh Playground-to-Test protocol. No project-wide license has been selected.

figure.alt: EmbodiedEvo method: Playground feedback evolves Skills and Lessons before a frozen harness transfers to fresh Test agents.
figure.credit: Wenyi Li et al., EmbodiedEvo: Self-Evolving Coding Agent For Physical Intelligence. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

related_releases.name: Learned Skills and Lessons for 42 RoboDojo tasks
related_releases.note: Released artifacts are available for reference and reuse; standard Playground/Test runs learn and freeze their own knowledge. The repository has not selected a project-wide license.

papers.title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
papers.summary: Studies whether robot agents retain useful skills and memories, and whether those improvements transfer across tasks, simulators, and real robots.
papers.loop: Run code-as-policy, agent-as-policy or VLA auto-research within fixed budgets → collect independent feedback → retain a cross-task library → evaluate against restarts and no-library controls on held-out conditions.
papers.setting: Simulation and real robot · 330 simulated tasks and five physical tasks
papers.evidence: SEAR compares code-as-policy, live agent-as-policy, and VLA auto-research modes across seven frontier models, 330 simulated tasks, and five physical tasks. Budget-matched controls distinguish retained experience from restarts, privileged information, and luck. The paper and project are public; the repository contains announcement assets and an unchecked code-release milestone, not an executable implementation.

figure.alt: SEAR Figure 2: code policies, live agents, and auto-research update a persistent library from simulation or hardware feedback.
figure.credit: Xinyi Wang et al., SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: RSI-Nav: Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement for Navigation via Policy-Synchronized Language-Action Dual Bootstrapping
papers.summary: Bootstraps navigation by generating instructions, filtering them through execution, and repeatedly updating the policy with the resulting data.
papers.loop: Generate language for unlabeled trajectories with the current policy → execute and filter by goal completion and efficiency → jointly update navigation and instruction generation with spatial replay → repeat per trajectory shard.
papers.setting: Simulation and real robot · R2R-CE, RxR-CE, DEEP Robotics M20
papers.evidence: Built on Qwen3.5-9B and evaluated on R2R-CE, RxR-CE, and a DEEP Robotics M20 robot. Released code covers training, trajectory conversion, recursive self-improvement, and R2R-CE evaluation; weights and datasets are prepared separately.

figure.alt: RSI-Nav Figure 3: the current policy generates instructions, filters them through execution, and updates after each trajectory shard.
figure.credit: Songze Li et al., RSI-Nav: Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement for Navigation via Policy-Synchronized Language-Action Dual Bootstrapping. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.summary: Builds a shared stateful code library through execution feedback, then runs robot tasks directly from code without model inference at test time.
papers.loop: Execute stateful code on development layouts → inspect measured state and failures → coding agents propose and test library diffs → retain improvements → run fixed code policies without model inference.
papers.setting: Simulation · 42 RoboDojo bimanual tasks
papers.evidence: Reports 70.24% success across RoboDojo’s 42 bimanual tasks. The authors identify accurate state measurement and robust code logic as key limitations.

figure.alt: COAP Figure 3: coding agents improve a shared stateful library offline; the final program controls the robot without model inference.
figure.credit: Kairui Hu et al., Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
papers.summary: Selects informative robot experiments to test hypotheses and improve executable code, reusable skills, and memory.
papers.loop: Maintain competing code/skill hypotheses → select informative physical experiments by value of information → co-evolve code and skills → consolidate reward-grounded hierarchical memory → improve subsequent adaptation.
papers.setting: Simulation and real robot · RoboCasa365, LIBERO-Pro; SO-101 arm with frozen SmolVLA
papers.evidence: The official project reports 77.0% overall RoboCasa365 success, 86.8% LIBERO-Pro, and 71.3% across five real-world tasks. The harness transfers from simulation; SmolVLA was first fine-tuned with 50 demonstrations per physical task and then frozen. Glasses-grasp success decreases from 60.0% to 56.7%.

figure.alt: EmbodiedRSI architecture: the Fast System tests code/skill hypotheses through a Hypothesis Graph while the Slow System consolidates hierarchical memory.
figure.credit: Python Song et al. (2026), EMBODIEDRSI method overview.

papers.title: EmbodiedSmith: Scaling Embodied Data through Recursive Self-Improvement Flywheel in Simulation
papers.summary: Uses simulation checks to revise task code, robot plans and scenes in a coupled generation loop. Accepted executions become demonstrations for training robot policies.
papers.loop: Generate a scene and task plan → run simulation and programmatic checks → review failures → revise scene/task code and robot plans → retain executable accepted tasks and trajectories for data generation.
papers.setting: Simulation data generation for mobile manipulators, humanoids and dexterous hands, including articulated, deformable and fluid interactions.
papers.evidence: The task-generation method explicitly runs and validates plans, routes failure diagnosis to task or scene revision, and checks executable delivery. Downstream experiments study generated-data diversity and generalization; they do not demonstrate an unconstrained robot modifying its own weights during deployment.

figure.alt: EmbodiedSmith Figure 3: Closed-loop robot task generation and validation. (a) Instructions are grounded in the scene, robot configuration, and available skills. (b) The Agent proposes a skill sequence and success conditions, which are used to build and compile a c
figure.credit: Yikai Qin et al., EmbodiedSmith, Figure 3.
figure.processing: Lossless WebP encoding; dimensions and decoded pixels unchanged.

papers.title: Co-Evolving Robot Orchestrators and Policies through Deployment
papers.summary: Curates demonstrations from deployment, selectively fine-tunes robot skills and adopts policies only after verification. The orchestrator updates its memories as the policy changes.
papers.loop: Execute with a mixed scripted/VLA orchestrator → curate skill-level demonstrations from successes and failures → selectively fine-tune recurring weak skills → verify target-skill gains and retention → adopt the candidate policy and continue deployment.
papers.setting: Ten simulated RoboLab tasks and three physical robot tasks.
papers.evidence: Author-reported held-out success is 64.8% to 73.8% in simulation and 38.3% to 50.0% on three physical tasks; unverified fixed-schedule fine-tuning reaches 65.8% in simulation. These are paper experiments, not RoboDojo leaderboard values. The project endpoint returned HTTP 403 at review, so no unverified Code/Data/Models links are shown.

figure.alt: Robo-COP Figure 2: The Robo-COP deployment-to-learning loop. A: The orchestrator mixes scripted motion and VLA calls, logs one action stream, and updates memory. B: Judges segment the stream into labeled skills; a controller decides when to train. C: Candidat
figure.credit: Xilun Zhang et al., Robo-COP, Figure 2.
figure.processing: Lossless WebP encoding; dimensions and decoded pixels unchanged.

papers.title: RobotUse: Allocating Computation, Context, and Decisions
papers.summary: A between-episode refiner turns robot execution reports into a persistent playbook. Later attempts reuse and revise guidance on spatial choices, recovery and task delegation.
papers.loop: Execute a task with subgoal reports → read main-agent trajectories between episodes → refine conditional guidance in a persistent playbook → reuse it in main and local decisions while keeping model parameters and backend code fixed.
papers.setting: RoboLab manipulation simulation and physical Franka Panda tasks.
papers.evidence: Section 4.4 explicitly retains experience across episodes; the refiner sees main-agent turns and local reports, rather than all low-level interaction details. The paper reports real-world learning and transfer under imperfect feedback. Code release runs native RoboLab episodes; external models, simulators and services are separate dependencies.

figure.alt: RobotUse Figure 1: RobotUse. The main agent decides in language: from the current state, the playbook, and returned reports, it issues an instruction. The subagent decides on the image, selecting points and poses that the robot backend plans and executes, and
figure.credit: Junhoo Lee et al., RobotUse, Figure 1. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
papers.summary: Reconstructs tasks in simulation, improves a shared skill library through practice and failure diagnosis, and transfers it to physical robots.
papers.loop: Reconstruct dataset tasks in simulation → practice and inspect execution video with privileged diagnostics → implement and cross-validate skill revisions → merge a shared library → freeze for physical deployment.
papers.setting: Simulation and real robot · 22 simulated tasks; 30 physical trials across three tasks
papers.evidence: Model weights stay fixed; privileged simulator state and dataset videos support offline diagnosis. Evaluated on 22 simulated tasks and 30 physical trials across three tasks after calibration and hardware adaptation. Code is listed as forthcoming.

figure.alt: RPG pipeline: runtime and privileged agents, video diagnosis, an implementor, and a merger improve a shared skill library.
figure.credit: Yen-Jen Wang et al., Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.name: PyRUA-Lean
papers.title: Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success Rate but 65% Fewer Tokens
papers.summary: Reduces repeated model calls by letting robot agents compose actions and local checks in Python. The repository also releases PyRUA-RSI’s offline-refined task programs, which run without language-model calls during evaluation.
papers.loop: The original paper studies efficient online code execution. The PyRUA-RSI extension reports an offline code-writing loop: execute candidate programs in RoboDojo, retain programs solving more episodes, and freeze them before evaluation.
papers.evidence: The matched-planner study covers 700 simulated instances across LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboCasa365. Token reductions apply to instances solved by both agents. The current verified RoboDojo snapshot is 55.26 Average Score and 50.35% Success Rate; the paper/project 58.20/51.62% experiment is a separate result and should not replace it. On 2026-10-30 the official repository released 54 fixed PyRUA-RSI task programs and an evaluation-only adapter. The author-reported development-seed results (82.82% success / 87.16 Score) and held-out seed-2 results (80.73% / 85.36) are separate from the official PyRUA-Lean leaderboard row. A dedicated technical report is forthcoming; the full improvement loop is not released.

figure.caption: Figure 2: composing primitives in Python cells with selective observation feedback.
figure.credit: Ruiyang Si, Jianxin Bi et al., PyRUA-Lean, Figure 2.
figure.alt: Figure 2: composing primitives in Python cells with selective observation feedback.

papers.source_catalogue: Awesome-Robot-Use-Agent README, matching PyRUA-Lean row; primary sources checked.
papers.setting: Simulation: LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo.

related_releases.name: PyRUA-RSI offline programs
related_releases.status: 54 task programs and evaluation adapter released; dedicated technical report forthcoming. This is an extension of PyRUA-Lean, not a new paper.

evaluation.source: author-reported RoboDojo evaluation, not the official PyRUA-Lean leaderboard row

related_releases.limitations: The released adapter is evaluation-only. The README describes offline candidate execution and retention, but the complete program-improvement loop is not released here.

papers.title: DynaHarness: A Dynamic Physical Harness for Self-Evolving Robot Agents
papers.summary: Attributes execution failures to reusable robot capabilities and proposes targeted repairs. Paired regression checks decide which revisions enter the shared physical harness.
papers.loop: Record bounded physical execution → attribute failures to a capability or mechanism → propose targeted revisions → compare parent and candidate with paired regression checks → admit validated capability updates.
papers.setting: LIBERO-Pro simulation, post-selection transfer tests and physical manipulation.
papers.evidence: Sections 3.6–3.7 and the attribution-driven self-evolution experiments distinguish reusable capability revision from within-episode monitoring. The reported 75.2% on 800 new initial states and 74.0% versus 63.9% dynamic-execution comparison use different experimental contrasts. The project-linked GitHub repository returned 404, so it is not advertised as released code.

figure.alt: DynaHarness Figure 2: Overview of DynaHarness . The slow brain plans; the fast brain governs execution; the offline loop evaluates updates from recorded evidence.
figure.credit: Haoyuan Deng et al., DynaHarness, Figure 2.

papers.title: ASENA: Self-evolving Agents for Embodied Navigation
papers.summary: Coding agents retain notes and executable skills after inspecting simulation feedback. A shared robot harness supports navigation, interaction and supervised physical execution without changing agent weights.
papers.loop: Run recurring navigation tasks → inspect simulator feedback → edit notes and executable skills → consolidate a persistent workspace → evaluate later passes with fixed model and policy weights.
papers.setting: Simulated R2R/RxR navigation and embodied question answering; supervised Unitree G1 demonstrations.
papers.evidence: The paper evaluates ten passes over recurring 100-task subsets: success rises from 72% to 98% on R2R and 65% to 89% on RxR. This measures repeated-task workspace evolution, not held-out task generalization. Physical demonstrations use supervised execution and do not establish the same autonomous learning gains on hardware.

figure.credit: An-Chieh Cheng et al., ASENA, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: Make Code as Policy Great Again: Frontier Agents Write, Call, and Evolve Robot Tools
papers.summary: A programming agent uses execution feedback and human guidance to refine reusable robot tools. A separate execution agent selects tools, with validated revisions kept across episodes.
papers.loop: Run development episodes → revise tool contracts, implementations and recovery from feedback and human guidance → validate and freeze accepted tools → reuse them in later execution episodes.
papers.setting: Five RoboDojo simulation tasks and seven physical AgileX dual-arm tasks.
papers.evidence: The paper explicitly preserves validated tool revisions across episodes with frozen foundation-model weights. Tool development includes human steering; reported execution-time and token savings exclude unmeasured authoring and steering costs. Five-task aggregate results are not the official all-task RoboDojo leaderboard.

figure.credit: Shijia Ge et al., URAI, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: RoboHarn-Evo: Evolving Hierarchical Physical Knowledge for Self-Improving Robotic Manipulation
papers.summary: Uses execution feedback to revise hierarchical task and action knowledge while keeping the base model and executor fixed.
papers.loop: Retrieve task/action knowledge → ground and execute skills → verify effects → reflect on recorded episodes → correct and consolidate hierarchical knowledge for future tasks.
papers.setting: Simulation and real robot · RMBench, frozen-knowledge RoboDojo transfer, physical manipulation
papers.evidence: Inner-loop retrieval grounds reusable knowledge in the current scene; outer-loop updates correct and consolidate it across episodes. Evaluated on RMBench, frozen-knowledge transfer to RoboDojo, and real-robot tasks. Public code includes the harness, knowledge maintenance, and benchmark adapters; simulator assets, model checkpoints, and services are configured separately.

figure.alt: RoboHarn-Evo method: task planning, grounded action, execution checks, and episode reflection evolve hierarchical knowledge.
figure.credit: Shifeng Bao et al., RoboHarn-Evo: Evolving Hierarchical Physical Knowledge for Self-Improving Robotic Manipulation. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: DexAgent: An Agentic Human2Sim2Robot Framework for Dexterous Manipulation with Self-Evolving Tool Library
papers.summary: Converts human videos into simulated robot demonstrations using property-specific checks to repair skills and verifiers. Newly developed tools remain in a library for later videos.
papers.loop: Interpret a human video → reconstruct simulation and optimize robot trajectories → use property-specific verifier feedback to refine stages → retain new skills and verifiers → reuse the enlarged tool library on subsequent videos.
papers.setting: Human2Sim2Robot dexterous data generation and policy evaluation across eleven physical tasks.
papers.evidence: The paper explicitly retains newly developed skills and verifiers and studies processing efficiency as more human videos are encountered. Policies are trained from accepted synthetic trajectories. This is tool-library growth in a data-generation workflow, not evidence that the deployed policy independently edits its own weights.

papers.title: Recursive Harness Distillation across Agents for Robot Manipulation
papers.summary: Distills a strong agent’s robot experience into a playbook for a lighter agent, then refines the playbook using the recipient’s feedback.
papers.loop: A strong agent intervenes around a frozen VLA → distill experience into a playbook → lighter agent executes → use recipient feedback to revise the shared playbook.
papers.setting: Simulation and real robot · SimplerEnv Bridge and Franka Panda
papers.evidence: Agents edit instructions, attention, and proposed actions around a frozen VLA. Evaluated in SimplerEnv Bridge and on a physical Franka Panda without updating model parameters.

figure.alt: RHD Figure 1: a strong agent distills robot-intervention experience into a playbook refined with a lighter agent’s feedback.
figure.credit: Seungyeon Kim et al., Recursive Harness Distillation across Agents for Robot Manipulation. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: RoboFoundry: System-as-Policy Evolution for Self-Learning Embodied Agents
papers.summary: Turns execution traces into tested changes to context, memory and hierarchical skills. Recurring repairs are promoted into a shared system for later tasks and robot embodiments.
papers.loop: Act and record traces → diagnose gaps in context or skills → propose task-specific system changes → check repair and retention on separate sets → promote recurring useful changes to the general system.
papers.setting: EmbodiedBench, RoboMemArena and LIBERO-PRO simulation, with physical transfer and online-evolution demonstrations.
papers.evidence: The method treats context and hierarchical skills as an evolvable system, with held-in repair and held-out retention checks before general promotion. Simulation benchmark gains and physical demonstrations are different evidence. The public repository currently contains project materials and TODOs for implementation releases; no Code link is shown.

figure.credit: Jingsong Liang et al., RoboFoundry, Figure 2.

papers.title: HarnessPAI: An Evolving Harness for Physical AI
papers.summary: Executes fixed robot programs within each rollout, then uses failure feedback to revise code between rollouts. Validated programs and repair skills are kept for reuse and demonstration generation.
papers.loop: Execute a fixed task program → collect outcome evidence → diagnose and revise candidate programs between rollouts → validate before promotion → retain code and structured skills, and generate demonstrations from converged programs.
papers.setting: Desktop manipulation, household simulation, robot-vacuum and legged settings, with downstream VLA/WAM interfaces.
papers.evidence: The paper distinguishes fixed program-level execution from closed-loop evolution across rollouts. The current official repository includes harness implementation, configurations, scripts and examples; its README describes candidate validation and reusable skill promotion. Reported downstream fine-tuning is a separate stage from coding-agent harness evolution.

figure.alt: HarnessPAI Figure 1: Overview of HarnessPAI , a general physical harness framework.
figure.credit: Xin Wang et al., HarnessPAI, Figure 1.
figure.processing: Lossless WebP encoding; dimensions and decoded pixels unchanged.

papers.title: RACaP: Agentic Reasoning, Acting, and Coding as Policies for Evolvable Robot Learning
papers.summary: Evolves typed robot APIs, a ReAct harness and experience memory through a capability curriculum and paired candidate tests. Deployment reuses frozen APIs while visual reasoning adapts their arguments.
papers.loop: Build capability APIs through a curriculum → diagnose rollout failures with a visual critic → propose reusable API/harness/memory edits → compare parent and candidate on matched tasks and budgets → freeze accepted code for deployment.
papers.setting: LIBERO-90, zero-shot LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-Long simulation; a separate decision-distillation study.
papers.evidence: The paper and released evolution implementation separate autonomous pre-deployment evolution from frozen runtime code. Runtime recovery does not rewrite APIs. Source release includes runtime and evolution code but excludes external model weights, training datasets and raw trajectories.

figure.credit: Zexi Li et al., RACaP, Figure 1.

papers.title: Zetta ζ: An Efficient Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence
papers.summary: Improves runtime critics and recovery skills from execution feedback around a frozen robot policy.
papers.loop: Execute a frozen policy with runtime critics → diagnose failure → evolve critic and recovery skills → gate updates → reuse validated interventions.
papers.setting: Simulation · LIBERO-Pro Goal and LIBERO-10 perturbations; 18 RoboCasa Atomic-Seen tasks
papers.evidence: With the base VLA frozen, the official project reports 90.8% mean success on LIBERO-Pro Goal (T/S) and 93.6% across 18 RoboCasa Atomic-Seen tasks under its rollout budget. These are simulation results; Goal success is distinct from the lower LIBERO-10 results, and task/rollout budgets should be matched in comparisons.

figure.alt: Zetta Z-Harness framework: execution feedback evolves runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen policy.
figure.credit: Xin Ding et al., Zetta ζ: An Efficient Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: SHAPER: Self-Evolving Embodied Agents via Skill-Harness Evolution
papers.summary: Uses rollout diagnosis to evolve reusable skills and the agent’s context-code harness without updating model weights.
papers.loop: Collect target-environment rollouts → diagnose round/episode failures into textual gradients → evolve skills then context-code harness → sandbox validation and top-K selection.
papers.setting: Simulation · VLABench and ESI-Bench
papers.evidence: Evaluated on VLABench and ESI-Bench with different action interfaces. Improves external skills and execution context without model training.

figure.alt: SHAPER Figure 2: rollout diagnosis produces textual gradients for sequential skill and harness evolution with sandbox validation and selection.
figure.credit: Peidong Wang et al., SHAPER: Self-Evolving Embodied Agents via Skill-Harness Evolution. Core method figure from the official paper/project.

papers.title: PhyAgentOS: A Self-Evolving Operating System for Embodied Agents with Decoupled Cognitive Planning and Physical Execution
papers.summary: Turns verified robot sessions into reusable skills and corrective lessons. File-based state and memory connect planning, supervised execution and later task attempts.
papers.loop: Compile a goal into an executable session → supervise physical execution and collect evidence → verify semantic completion → consolidate reusable knowledge, corrective lessons and skills → retrieve them for subsequent sessions.
papers.setting: Simulation, games and physical-robot validation over heterogeneous embodiments; manipulation evaluations include LIBERO, CALVIN and RoboCasa365.
papers.evidence: The runtime distinguishes execution termination from task success and retains verified experience through epistemic memory without retraining. Games, simulator benchmarks and hardware demonstrations are separate validation levels; support across embodiments is not equivalent to independently reproduced autonomous RSI gains.

figure.credit: Yang Liu et al., PhyAgentOS, Figure 3.

papers.title: ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
papers.summary: Discovers reusable robot /skills by writing programs, diagnosing execution traces, repairing failures, and retaining successful strategies.
papers.loop: Execute candidate programs → diagnose multimodal traces → repair and validate code → save reusable /skills for subsequent tasks.
papers.setting: LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K simulation; selected physical-robot transfer experiments.
papers.evidence: Evaluated on LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K, with simulation-to-real skill transfer and online physical-robot examples including Rubik’s Cube manipulation. The project distinguishes debug seeds from held-out evaluation seeds. Behavior is bounded by a predefined perception, planning and control API. The real-world setup still requires success detection, resets, monitoring and calibration; reported performance depends on the language model, task subset and evaluation protocol.

figure.alt: ASPIRE system overview: execution traces, agentic program search and a reusable skill library (Figure 1).
figure.credit: Runyu Lu et al., ASPIRE, arXiv:2607.00272v2, Figure 1. CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
papers.summary: Automates real-world policy improvement through repeated robot resets, execution, outcome verification, and revisions to policy or training code.
papers.loop: Reset and execute → verify outcomes and inspect logs → revise policy code or training → evaluate the revision and retain improvements.
papers.setting: Physical robot manipulation and RoboCasa simulation.
papers.evidence: Real-world manipulation includes Push-T, pin insertion, GPU insertion and zip-tie tasks, with additional RoboCasa simulation. The project page defines its headline 99% result as pass@8 with adaptive in-context retries; it should not be presented as 99% single-attempt success. Requires calibrated stations and task-specific reset and outcome-verification functions. Robot-fleet speedups consume additional tokens and depend on resource utilization.

figure.alt: ENPIRE physical autoresearch framework and real-world task overview (Figure 2).
figure.credit: Wenli Xiao et al., ENPIRE, arXiv:2606.19980v2, Figure 2. CC BY 4.0.

leaderboard.freshness_note: updated_at is the timestamp declared in the official JavaScript bundle; checked_at is the date these rankings were verified.
leaderboard.metric: Average Score (descending); Success Rate (%) shown separately
leaderboard.protocol: RoboDojo-Sim Agent track; 42 simulation tasks in Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon, Memory, and Open. Includes Agent, Agent + WAM and Agent + VLA entries. Score is a progress metric, not success rate; Generalization averages standard and random layouts. The site sorts Average Score descending, then Success Rate descending, then model name; display ranks are ordinal. No ties affect the retained agent ranks.
